answers_by_date.answer: any conviction (even minor administrative offenses) can lead to loss of residence status
answers_by_date.basis: Ley 22.439 (1981) was in force. Art. 95(a) allowed the Interior Ministry to expel 'todo extranjero, cualquiera sea su situación de residencia' convicted of an intentional crime carrying more than 5 years, subject to the family/10-year waiver in art. 96. Art. 38 separately allowed cancellation of temporary, transitory or precarious residence, and expulsion, of any foreigner 'que no cumpla o viole las disposiciones de la presente y de las respectivas reglamentaciones', so a mere breach of the migration rules could cost non-permanent residents their status. This is the lowest option, so implementation does not apply. It differs from 2005 because Ley 25.871 replaced Ley 22.439 on 21 January 2004.

answers_by_date.answer: only major convictions (e.g., criminal offenses) can lead to loss of residence status
answers_by_date.basis: Original Ley 25.871 (in force 21 Jan 2004), art. 62(b): residence is cancelled only where the resident was 'condenado judicialmente en la República por delito doloso que merezca pena privativa de libertad mayor de cinco (5) años' or showed repeated offending. Even then the decision waits two years after the sentence is served, and a waiver applies for a parent, child or spouse of an Argentine (art. 62, final paragraphs). Art. 29(c) made convictions for 3+ year offences an impediment for applicants. No regulation existed yet, and Decreto 1023/94 survived only where compatible (art. 124). No practice source for this period could be read (the CELS 2005 report is a PDF the tool could not open), so the rating is a low-confidence inference for a law still in transition.

answers_by_date.answer: only major convictions (e.g., criminal offenses) can lead to loss of residence status
answers_by_date.basis: Same original art. 62(b) and art. 29(c) of Ley 25.871. Decreto 616/2010, which regulates art. 62, entered into force only in July 2010, after this date. The CMW concluding observations of 2011 (practice around 2010) criticise DNM for ignoring family and personal circumstances when it orders expulsion on art. 29 impediments, mostly for lack of proof of legal entry. They do not report convicted residents losing status for minor offences.

answers_by_date.answer: only major convictions (e.g., criminal offenses) can lead to loss of residence status
answers_by_date.basis: Original arts. 29 and 62 of Ley 25.871, with Decreto 616/2010 art. 62 (courts send final convictions to DNM), stood unamended until DNU 70/2017 replaced art. 62 from 31 Jan 2017. That decree lets any conviction for an offence punishable by imprisonment, even a non-final one, cancel residence, which explains the 2020 answer. Practice: official DNM figures reported by La Nación show 239 deportations in 2015 and 1,256 across 2011–2015, against about 3,000 in 2016–2019. Removals of convicted residents were limited before the 2017 decree.

answers.change_2000_2020: There have been no right protections neither in 2000 nor in 2020

answers.repealed_search: Searched for a protection that existed between 2000 and 2020 and was later narrowed. Compared the original text of Ley 25.871 (InfoLEG norma.htm) with DNU 70/2017. Original art. 62(b) (2004 to 30 Jan 2017) allowed cancellation only for intentional crimes carrying more than 5 years or repeated offending, with waivers. DNU 70/2017 art. 6 replaced it from 31 Jan 2017 with cancellation for any offence punishable by imprisonment, even without a final conviction. Under Ley 22.439 (to Jan 2004), art. 95 already used the >5-year threshold for expulsion, but art. 38 allowed non-permanent residence to be cancelled for any breach of the migration rules.

answers.starting_answer_concern: DNU 70/2017 tied cancellation to offences 'que merezcan ... penas privativas de la libertad', that is criminal offences. Administrative offences and contraventions were not grounds. So 'only major convictions (criminal offenses)' would also be a defensible reading for 2020. The lowest option is understandable, given that any imprisonable crime, even with a non-final conviction, triggered automatic cancellation.
answers.notes: The 2000 answer rests on Ley 22.439 art. 38, which let non-permanent residence be cancelled for any breach of the migration law or its regulations. Art. 95 alone, which reached permanent residents and used the >5-year threshold, would support 'only major convictions'. A reviewer may prefer that reading. The CNACAF Sala V ruling of March 2018 declaring DNU 70/2017 unconstitutional (CELS y otros c/ EN) is known only from press reports. It was not read, and the decree stayed in force pending the Supreme Court. Decreto 138/2021 (March 2021) repealed the decree and restored the original text, which explains the MRD's 2023 'only major' answer.

answers_by_date.basis: Since 1994, Constitution art. 75(22) has given constitutional rank to the CAT. CAT art. 3 (approved by Ley 23.338) bars expulsion, return or extradition 'cuando haya razones fundadas para creer que estaría en peligro de ser sometida a tortura'. Ley 22.439 had no statutory non-refoulement clause, and refugee determination was done by CEPARE under decree. Practice evidence for this period is thin: the HRC 2000 concluding observations say nothing on refoulement, and the CERD 2004 findings of reported refoulement cover the early 2000s.

Same constitutional-rank treaty protection. Ley 25.871 (Jan 2004) added no explicit non-refoulement rule. CERD (Dec 2004) was 'concerned about reported cases of refoulement of refugees and allegedly unfair refugee status determination procedures' and noted there was no comprehensive refugee law. That evidence covers refugees and asylum seekers only.

Ley 26.165 (in force Dec 2006) art. 7 bars expelling, returning or extraditing refugees and pending asylum seekers where there is a risk to life, liberty or security, 'incluido el derecho a no ser sometido a tortura ni a otros tratos o penas crueles, inhumanos o degradantes'. Art. 39 makes every border and police official responsible for respecting it. Decreto 616/2010 art. 23(m) came only in July 2010. The State Department 2011 report found an established refugee protection system and cooperation with UNHCR, with no reports of refoulement.

Ley 26.165 arts. 2, 7 and 39, Decreto 616/2010 art. 23(m)(1)-(2) (humanitarian residence for people protected by non-refoulement who are not refugees) and the constitutional-rank CAT art. 3. The State Department 2015 report found a functioning asylum system and UNHCR cooperation, but decisions taking up to two years, with no refoulement reported. DNU 70/2017 (summary expulsion procedure), in force from 2017, explains the lower 2020 rating.

answers.change_2000_2020: There have been right protections both in 2000 and 2020 but they are not the same

answers.sourcing_note: Every past-date provision is unamended since enactment (Constitution 1994, Leyes 23.338 and 26.165, Decreto 616/2010), so the current text is the text in force on each date. Ley 22.439 was read in consolidated form. CEPARE decrees (Decreto 464/85) and the 1951 Convention approval (Ley 15.869) were not read. Practice evidence for 2000 is very thin and covers refugees only.
answers.notes: The 2000 and 2005 'Yes' rests on CAT art. 3, which has had constitutional rank under art. 75(22) since 1994 and is self-executing in Argentina's monist system. No statute or court ruling was relied on for those dates. Practice evidence covers refugees and asylum seekers. Nothing was found on migrants facing a torture risk outside the asylum system. The USCR 2001 report on CEPARE's attempt to block Roma asylum seekers was seen only in search results and is not relied on.

answers_by_date.basis: Constitution art. 75(22) gives constitutional rank to the ACHR, whose art. 22.8 (Ley 23.054) provides: 'En ningún caso el extranjero puede ser expulsado o devuelto a otro país ... donde su derecho a la vida o la libertad personal está en riesgo de violación a causa de raza, nacionalidad, religión, condición social o de sus opiniones políticas'. Refugee determination was done by CEPARE under decree, and Ley 22.439 had no statutory clause. Practice evidence is thin (HRC 2000 is silent), and CERD 2004 later reported refoulement cases.

Same constitutional-rank ACHR art. 22.8. Ley 25.871 did not codify non-refoulement. CERD (Dec 2004) reported 'cases of refoulement of refugees and allegedly unfair refugee status determination procedures'. Evidence covers refugees and asylum seekers.

Ley 26.165 (Dec 2006), art. 2: protection 'con arreglo a los principios de no devolución, incluyendo la prohibición de rechazo en frontera', applied to recognised refugees and applicants alike. Arts. 7 and 39 add the ban and make officials responsible for it. The State Department 2011 report found a working system and UNHCR cooperation, with no refoulement reported.

Ley 26.165 arts. 2, 7 and 39, Decreto 616/2010 art. 23(m) and ACHR art. 22.8. The State Department 2015 report found a functioning asylum system with decisions taking up to two years and no refoulement reported. The 2017 summary-expulsion decree explains the lower 2020 rating.

answers.sourcing_note: The cited provisions are unamended, so today's text is the past text. The 2000 and 2005 answers rest on constitutional-rank treaties, not statute, which makes them weaker; ACHR 22.8 ties the risk to life to discriminatory grounds. Practice for 2000 is very thin and refugee-only.
answers.starting_answer_concern: The citation lists Ley 26.165 art. 29, which concerns the appointment of CONARE's Executive Secretary and has nothing to do with non-refoulement. Art. 7 is the operative provision.
answers.notes: Coding 2000 and 2005 as 'Yes' assumes that ACHR art. 22.8 (risk to life or liberty) and CAT art. 3, both of constitutional rank, amount to a ban on return to serious deprivations of fundamental rights. A stricter reviewer could code 'No' before Ley 26.165 (Dec 2006), since no general life-risk ground independent of the persecution grounds existed in national law until then. No ruling was relied on.
